text.p: Guatemala's December peace accord with leftist guerrillas has not stopped the country's plague of lynchings. Angry mobs have burned nine Guatemalans alive in the first two weeks of 1997 alone.

On Jan. 1, only three days after Guatemalans celebrated the signing of pacts ending 36 years of guerrilla war, an enraged mob burned two men suspected of robbing businesses near the town of Solola, 75 miles (125 kms) from the capital.

An American church worker who did not want to give his name told Reuters he saw one of the men, consumed in flames, run screaming into the middle of the Panamerican Highway where he managed to extinguish the flames.
The crowd of hundreds, including young children, chased the presumed thief, doused him with fuel and set him on fire again. He died in the highway, the witness said.
The witness said nervous policemen tried in vain to calm the crowd before the lynching. No one was arrested.

Three lynchings occurred in other rural towns during the first two weeks of the year and police sources said four suspected robbers were lynched early on Wednesday near the town of San Juan Sacatepequez, 34 miles (56 km) from the capital.
Accounts of their deaths varied but lynch mobs in Guatemala typically burn, beat or hack their victims to death.

The mob violence highlights challenges facing Guatemala as it tries to repair its weak justice system and other institutions after the historic peace treaty between the government and leftist rebels. The agreement ended a guerrilla war and brutal counterinsurgency campaigns that left more than 140,000 dead or missing.

Frustrated with the inept justice system, many Guatemalans say crime and punishment are of more concern to them than peace. In some cases, enraged crowds dragged accused thieves out of local jails and killed them.

Dinorah Azpuru, political analyst with the Social Studies and Research Association think tank, told Reuters lynchings were not affected by the peace accords. She said poorer people become enraged because their few possessions have been targets for criminals who no longer prey exclusively on the rich.

"But it is probably also an effect of 36 years of armed conflict in which dialogue and peaceful resolution of conflicts has not been taught. Under authoritarian regimes the use of force has been the way to control things," Azpuru said.
Authorities have not arrested or charged anyone in connection with the dozens of lynchings and attempted lynchings in 1996.

Fernando Linares, a prominent Guatemalan lawyer, told Reuters lynchings were very difficult to investigate. "Almost the entire population (involved) agrees with the lynching. It is a collective act. So it is very difficult to find proof or someone to accuse the people who did the lynching."

Newspapers said pealing church bells called hundreds of people to the lynching of four men on Wednesday near San Juan Sacatepequez. "The whole town" was involved, National Police spokesman Francisco Simon Borror told Reuters. The incident went on for hours as the mob tried to question the four men.
"It seems as though this town was tired of so many robberies. They captured these guys and they took justice into their own hands," Borror said.

The four men, one dressed in a fake police officer's uniform, were accused by the townspeople of setting up a "checkpoint" on the dirt highway leading into the town where they stopped and robbed drivers, he said. After they were killed, the mob burned their bodies.
